{{Short description|Mathematical notation for tensors and spinors}}
{{distinguish|tensor index notation}}

'''Abstract index notation''' (also referred to as slot-naming index notation)<ref name="Thorne2017">{{Cite book |last=Kip S. Thorne and Roger D. Blandford |title=Modern Classical Physics: Optics, Fluids, Plasmas, Elasticity, Relativity, and Statistical Physics |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=2017 |isbn=978-0-69115902-7}}</ref> is a mathematical notation for [[tensor]]s and [[spinor]]s that uses indices to indicate their types, rather than their components in a particular basis.<ref name="Penrose2007">{{Cite book |last=Roger Penrose |title=The Road to Reality: A Complete Guide to the Laws of the Universe |publisher=Vintage |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-67977631-4}}</ref> The indices are mere placeholders, not related to any basis and, in particular, are non-numerical. Thus it should not be confused with the [[Ricci calculus]]. The notation was introduced by [[Roger Penrose]] as a way to use the formal aspects of the [[Einstein summation convention]] to compensate for the difficulty in describing [[tensor contraction|contraction]]s and [[covariant derivative|covariant differentiation]] in modern abstract tensor notation, while preserving the explicit [[Covariance and contravariance of vectors|covariance]] of the expressions involved.<ref name="Penrose1984">{{Cite book |author1=Roger Penrose|author2=[[Wolfgang Rindler]] |title=Spinors and Space-Time, Volume 1: Two-Spinor Calculus and Relativistic Fields |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1984 |isbn=978-0-52133707-6}}</ref>

Let <math>V</math> be a [[vector space]], and <math>V^*</math> its [[dual space]].  Consider, for example, an order-2 [[Covariance and contravariance of vectors|covariant]] tensor <math>h \in V^*\otimes V^*</math>.  Then <math>h</math> can be identified with a [[bilinear form]] on <math>V</math>.  In other words, it is a function of two arguments in <math>V</math> which can be represented as a pair of ''slots'':
: <math>h = h(-,-).</math>

Abstract index notation is merely a ''labelling'' of the slots with Latin letters, which have no significance apart from their designation as labels of the slots (i.e., they are non-numerical):
: <math>h = h_{ab}.</math>

A [[tensor contraction]] (or trace) between two tensors is represented by the repetition of an index label, where one label is contravariant (an ''upper index'' corresponding to the factor <math>V</math>) and one label is covariant (a ''lower index'' corresponding to the factor <math>V^*</math>).  Thus, for instance,
: <math>t_{ab}{}^b</math>

is the trace of a tensor <math>t = t_{ab}{}^c</math> over its last two slots.  This manner of representing tensor contractions by repeated indices is formally similar to the [[Einstein summation convention]].  However, as the indices are non-numerical, it does not imply summation: rather it corresponds to the abstract basis-independent trace operation (or [[natural pairing]]) between tensor factors of type <math>V</math> and those of type <math>V^*</math>.

== Abstract indices and tensor spaces ==

A general homogeneous tensor is an element of a [[tensor product]] of copies of <math>V</math> and <math>V^*</math>, such as

:<math>V \otimes V^* \otimes V^* \otimes V \otimes V^*.</math>

Label each factor in this tensor product with a Latin letter in a raised position for each contravariant <math>V</math> factor, and in a lowered position for each covariant <math>V^*</math> position.  In this way, write the product as
:<math>V^a V_b V_c V^d V_e</math>
or, simply
:<math>V^a{}_{bc}{}^d{}_e.</math>

The last two expressions denote the same object as the first.  Tensors of this type are denoted using similar notation, for example:
:<math>h^a{}_{bc}{}^d{}_e \in V^a{}_{bc}{}^d{}_e = V \otimes V^* \otimes V^* \otimes V \otimes V^*.</math>

== Contraction ==
{{See also|Tensor contraction}}
In general, whenever one contravariant and one covariant factor occur in a tensor product of spaces, there is an associated ''contraction'' (or ''trace'') map.  For instance,
: <math>\mathrm{Tr}_{12} : V \otimes V^* \otimes V^* \otimes V \otimes V^* \to V^* \otimes V \otimes V^*</math>
is the trace on the first two spaces of the tensor product.<math display="block">\mathrm{Tr}_{15} : V \otimes V^* \otimes V^* \otimes V \otimes V^* \to V^* \otimes V^* \otimes V</math> is the trace on the first and last space.

These trace operations are signified on tensors by the repetition of an index.  Thus the first trace map is given by
: <math>\mathrm{Tr}_{12} : h{}^a{}_b{}_c{}^d{}_e \mapsto h{}^a{}_a{}_c{}^d{}_e</math>
and the second by
: <math>\mathrm{Tr}_{15} : h{}^a{}_b{}_c{}^d{}_e \mapsto h{}^a{}_b{}_c{}^d{}_a.</math>

== Braiding ==
To any tensor product on a single vector space, there are associated [[Tensor product#Tensor powers and braiding|braiding maps]].  For example, the braiding map
:<math> \tau_{(12)} : V \otimes V \rightarrow V \otimes V</math>
interchanges the two tensor factors (so that its action on simple tensors is given by <math>\tau_{(12)} (v \otimes w) = w \otimes v</math>).  In general, the braiding maps are in one-to-one correspondence with elements of the [[symmetric group]], acting by permuting the tensor factors.  Here, <math>\tau_\sigma</math> denotes the braiding map associated to the permutation <math>\sigma</math> (represented as a product of disjoint [[cyclic permutation]]s).

Braiding maps are important in [[differential geometry]], for instance, in order to express the [[Bianchi identity]].  Here let <math>R</math> denote the [[Riemann curvature tensor|Riemann tensor]], regarded as a tensor in <math>V^* \otimes V^* \otimes V^* \otimes V</math>.  The first Bianchi identity then asserts that
:<math>R + \tau_{(123)}R + \tau_{(132)}R = 0.</math>

Abstract index notation handles braiding as follows.  On a particular tensor product, an ordering of the abstract indices is fixed (usually this is a [[lexicographic order]]ing).  The braid is then represented in notation by permuting the labels of the indices.  Thus, for instance, with the Riemann tensor
:<math>R = R_{abc}{}^d \in V_{abc}{}^d = V^* \otimes V^* \otimes V^* \otimes V,</math>

the Bianchi identity becomes
:<math>R_{abc}{}^d + R_{cab}{}^d + R_{bca}{}^d = 0.</math>

== Antisymmetrization and symmetrization ==
A general tensor may be antisymmetrized or symmetrized, and there is according notation.

We demonstrate the notation by example. Let's antisymmetrize the type-(0,3) tensor <math>\omega_{abc}</math>, where <math>\mathrm{S}_3</math> is the symmetric group on three elements.
: <math>\omega_{[abc]} := \frac{1}{3!} \sum_{\sigma \in \mathrm{S}_3} {\text{sgn}(\sigma)} \omega_{\sigma(a)\sigma(b)\sigma(c)}</math>

Similarly, we may symmetrize:
: <math>\omega_{(abc)} := \frac{1}{3!} \sum_{\sigma \in \mathrm{S}_3} \omega_{\sigma(a)\sigma(b)\sigma(c)}</math>
